steps.observation: Work on this for 60 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the key differences between DNA and RNA:

1. Sugar backbone  
   • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) contains deoxyribose, which lacks an oxygen atom on the 2′ carbon.  
   • RNA (ribonucleic acid) contains ribose, which has a hydroxyl (–OH) group on the 2′ carbon.  
   – That extra –OH makes RNA more reactive and less chemically stable than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).  
   • RNA uses A, G, C and uracil (U) in place of thymine.

3. Strandedness and structure  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming the famous right-handed double helix.  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded, though it can fold back on itself to form hairpins or more complex 3D shapes.

4. Location and function  
   • DNA resides primarily in the cell nucleus (in eukaryotes) and stores the organism’s long-term genetic blueprint.  
   • RNA is made in the nucleus (or nucleoid in bacteria) but travels to the cytoplasm and comes in several forms (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, etc.) to  
     – carry coding instructions (mRNA),  
     – help assemble amino acids (tRNA),  
     – form the core of ribosomes (rRNA),  
     – or regulate gene expression (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA).

5. Stability and lifespan  
   • DNA’s deoxyribose-based, double-stranded structure makes it very stable—ideal for archival storage of genetic information.  
   • RNA is more prone to hydrolysis (the 2′-OH can attack its own backbone), giving it a shorter lifespan—suitable for transient information transfer and regulation.

Summary  
DNA is the long-term, double-stranded repository of genetic information built on deoxyribose and thymine. RNA is a more versatile, single-stranded molecule with ribose and uracil, specialized for carrying, translating and regulating genetic messages.
